episodes.title: King Sejong the Great and Hangeul

subtitle.text: From the time he was a child, King Sejong loved to read.
As a young prince, he read through the bitterly cold nights in winter.
He read through the hot, humid nights in summer.
He read every book in the palace, and some he read many times. The
prince loved to read so much that his father, King Taejong, worried for his son's health. He
ordered the removal of all books from his son's room. One
book, however, was accidentally left behind. The
young prince found it and and read it over and over again. Seeing
this, King Taejong realized that he couldn't stop his son from reading. So
he gave up and returned the prince's books. When
he became king in 1418, Sejong was still thinking about books. He understood
that books were a powerful tool to educate his people. Agriculture was
very important to the country, so he was dismayed that there were no modern books on farming. And there
weren't any books written for farmers in Korea. The king
ordered scholars to travel the kingdom and study local farming practices. The scholars
compiled their knowledge into the Nongsajikseol ( Plain Explanation of Farming Matters ).
The book was distributed to government offices throughout the country, along with the king's personal wish for it to help farmers. The
king not only hoped to improve the kingdom's economic well-being but also his subjects' moral well-being. In
1432, the Samganghaengsildo ( Guide to the Three Relationships ) was
published. This book explained the relationships between subjects and kings, children and parents, and husbands and
wives. These were the most important human relationships, according to thinking at the
time. It included illustrations so that everyone could learn from the book—even those who couldn't
read. The king was also determined to increase literacy in his kingdom.
At the time very few men, and even fewer women, were literate.
Only elite people like nobles, officials, and scholars could read and write.
The Korean language was written using Chinese characters, hanja
, which were difficult to learn and did not reflect the sounds of the Korean language
well. If most people could not read or write, books had no meaning for
them. The well-educated court officials didn't mind
this. Reading and writing gave them power.
However, the king had long recognized that this was a problem—and he liked to solve problems.
Anticipating that the palace elite would oppose him, the king secretly began to work on a way to spread literacy to all his people.
He had an ambitious goal: he wanted to create a new writing system.
He carefully studied Chinese characters and their sounds.
He analyzed the sounds of the Korean language and the way people's speech organs make those sounds.
He also examined different writing systems for ideas. Though
the king worked in secret, he received help from his son, Crown Prince Munjong, and possibly his other children as well. When
his writing system was completed in 1443, the king unveiled his alphabet of 28 letters to the court as his personal creation. He
called his writing system Hunminjeongeum , which means "Correct Sounds for the Instruction of People."
The king's letters were simple and elegant.
The designs of the consonants were based on the shapes of human speech organs when making these sounds. The
vowel shapes were meant to represent the earth, the heavens, and humans. Best
of all, the system was designed to be easy for anyone to learn. The
king was pleased with his creation, but the court officials were not. Nonetheless,
when the king ordered scholars to help him, they had no choice. King
Sejong created the Eonmuncheong , an office devoted to working on the alphabet.
Its first task was to develop a guide to the alphabet.
Meanwhile the king had turned his attention to using the new alphabet. In
1444 he wanted to publish the Samganghaengsildo again, this time using his new alphabet. But
the project didn't take place during his lifetime. The
next year he oversaw the publication of the Yongbieocheonga ( Songs of the Dragons Flying to Heaven
). This book celebrates the king's ancestors and was the first new book written with the king's
alphabet. After several years the Eonmuncheong scholars completed a document entitled
Hunminjeongeum . It was released on October 9, 1446, and contained an introduction written by the king, like a letter to the
people: Because our nation's speech is different from that of China, hanja are not suited for
it. Therefore illiterate people who wish to learn encounter great difficulty, and their ability to communicate is
limited. This saddened me, so I have created 28 new
letters. I wish for all to learn and use them, and they be convenient for daily
use. Just as King Sejong wished, his new alphabet caught on with commoners and women of all classes.
But scholars and elites were still using hanja when King Sejong died in 1450.
Slowly, over the centuries, more and more people used King Sejong's alphabet for everyday communication and published works.
Even the upper classes used it, though they never fully abandoned hanja
. Despite the growing popularity of the alphabet, at various times it was
outlawed. However, by the twentieth century, King Sejong's alphabet was widespread and had become known as
Hangeul. Every year on October 9, Hangeul Day celebrates the gift of King Sejong's alphabet to the public.
Hangeul continues to be admired around the world as a unique writing system.
And it remains King Sejong the Great's lasting and most important legacy.
Jesse dropped his backpack on the kitchen counter with a sigh.
His mother looked up from her laptop. "Bad day?"
"Sort of," Jesse muttered.
"Career Day is next week, and the principal selected me to introduce one of the speakers.
It's an honor to get selected, but I wanted to introduce the professional soccer player, not Dr. Devarti."
"Really?" Jesse's mom sounded surprised.
"Dr. Devarti has a fascinating career with Doctors Without Borders—and you've known her for years."
"I know her from our neighborhood," Jesse said.
"But I don't know anything about her career."
"Why don't you give her a call and see if you can interview her?" his mom suggested.
Thirty minutes later Jesse found himself trudging toward Dr. Devarti's house.
"Come on in," Dr. Devarti said.
"My kids are working on their homework, so it's a convenient time to talk."
"Cool room," Jesse thought as he entered a spacious family room.
Tall bookshelves stuffed with books and interesting objects stretched from floor to ceiling.
Other shelves held African masks, bronze bells, and dolls dressed in costumes.
He picked up a colorful woven basket.
"That was made by a woman in Sudan," Dr. Devarti said.
"My first posting after joining Doctors Without Borders was in Darfur, Sudan."
"Thanks for letting me ask you about Doctors Without Borders," Jesse began.
"I need to write a brief introduction before you speak at our Career Day assembly.
So I'd like to get some background information."
"Sure," Dr. Devarti said.
"Working for Doctors Without Borders has changed my life—and even the way that I practice medicine."
Jesse took notes as the physician explained that Doctors Without Borders had been founded in 1971 in France.
A group of doctors and journalists were troubled by the way politics sometimes interfered with aid for victims of disaster and disease.
So the group decided to create a new relief organization that could deliver free and rapid medical care to people affected by war, epidemics, and disasters.
In 1999 the organization received the Nobel Peace Prize.
"Doctors Without Borders is known as Médecins Sans Frontières in some parts of the world," Dr. Devarti went on.
"It's an impartial humanitarian organization, which means we treat people without considering things like race, religion, or politics."
"Are all the workers volunteers?" Jesse asked.
"No, everyone has to apply to work for Doctors Without Borders—and get hired.
You're paid a salary, and there are some requirements.
For example, you have to be able to travel on a mission for nine to twelve months at a time.
You also have to possess the right personality and be flexible.
Workers often face hardships, like living on a boat, in a war zone, or in a city destroyed by an earthquake.
Doctors and nurses see many heartbreaking situations, so you also have to be able to cope with that.
And it's an asset if you're proficient in more than one language."
"Wow," Jesse said, "that sounds intense."
Dr. Devarti nodded.
"It's dangerous too, especially when you're working in a war zone or treating patients with deadly infectious diseases like cholera."
Jesse skimmed his notes.
"You said Doctors Without Borders delivers rapid medical care.
But its patients live all over the world.
How can medical workers get to these places quickly?"
"Good question. Doctors Without Borders has over thirty thousand workers in about seventy countries.
And there are hubs all over the world, so they can mobilize medical teams quickly and efficiently.
The hubs are stocked with reserves of prepackaged kits containing medicine and supplies—even inflatable tents for surgical procedures."
"Whoa," Jesse said, "you can perform surgery outdoors in the middle of a disaster area?"
Dr. Devarti nodded. "We sure can. It allows us to save many lives."
"What was the hardest mission you've ever been on?" Jesse asked.
"Hmm . . . " Dr. Devarti thought for a moment.
"Last year I worked on a medical boat in the Mediterranean Sea.
Conditions at sea were rough, and we were treating refugees who had fled their home countries by boat.
Many of our patients were kids whose parents had drowned."
"I see what you mean about heartbreaking," Jesse murmured.
"I can't imagine losing my parents as well as my home.
One final question: what do you like best about working for Doctors Without Borders?"
Dr. Devarti smiled. "That's an easy one—I've traveled all over the world and met lots of interesting people.
I've also learned to stay calm in medical emergencies and listen carefully, especially to patients from different cultures.
Working for Doctors Without Borders has been very rewarding, and it's made me a much better doctor."
Jesse shook his head, awed by what he'd learned about Dr. Devarti's career.
Earlier today he'd been worried about introducing her at the assembly.
Now he was eager to share details about her impressive career!

episodes.title: Terry Fox: The Marathon of Hope

subtitle.text: One of Canada's greatest heroes never fought a war.
He was not a scientist, and he was never a political leader.
However, by running in what he called the Marathon of Hope, Terry Fox made the entire country proud.
Terry Fox grew up in the town of Port Coquitlam, near the city of Vancouver.
Terry was an extremely active and diligent child.
From a very early age, no matter what he did, he always worked hard and tried to do his best.
Terry especially loved to compete and play sports.
In high school he wanted to play on the basketball team, but he was too short, and he was a terrible player.
However, that didn't discourage him. Instead Terry started getting up early each morning to practice his basketball skills.
By tenth grade Terry had improved so much, he earned a spot on the high school team!
By his senior year, he was considered one of the best basketball players— and athletes—in the whole school.
In 1977, when he was just 18 years old, Terry faced another difficult challenge.
Doctors discovered that he had bone cancer.
In order to save his life, his right leg would have to be amputated above the knee.
On the night before his amputation, a former coach brought Terry an article about amputee runners.
Inspired by the story, Terry decided that he would also learn to run one day.
Being in the hospital affected Terry deeply.
All around him were children in pain and others who were dying.
It was hard for him to watch this suffering without doing anything.
So soon Terry had a new dream: first he would learn how to run with his artificial leg.
Then he would run all the way across Canada.
It would be a "Marathon of Hope" to collect money to help cancer patients.
Wherever he went, Terry told people about his Marathon of Hope.
He explained that he wanted to collect one dollar from every person in Canada to help find a cure for cancer.
If he met his goal, he could raise 24 million dollars— a lot of money for cancer research!
He said he was determined to take himself to the limit for this cause.
Most people thought that Terry's dream was impossible.
Canada is a huge country; to run from one end to the other meant running thousands of miles!
Plus, Terry was recovering from cancer and had an artificial leg.
How could he possibly accomplish such a difficult feat? But Terry was once again determined.
After more than one year of intense training, he was finally ready to run.
On April 12, 1980, he stood in St. John, Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada, and dipped his artificial leg in the Atlantic Ocean.
Then he filled two large bottles with ocean water.
He wanted to keep one bottle as a souvenir.
He planned to pour the other bottle into the Pacific Ocean when he reached the west coast at the end of his run!
Terry's marathon started as a very low-key event.
He ran alone, though a friend was with him to help with cooking and to drive the van where he slept some nights.
It was not an easy journey. Terry ran through ice storms, summer heat, and fierce winds.
Each day he ran an average of 42 kilometers.
Sometimes he fell down from exhaustion or pain.
At first a small number of people supported Terry and his quest.
But as he ran westward along his course, more and more people learned about his dream.
Soon people were lining the roads along his route, shouting his name and cheering him on.
In some towns schoolchildren ran with him.
Donations from people inspired by his strength and his courage poured in.
After running for 143 days and 5,373 kilometers, Terry felt pain in his chest and he was forced to stop in Thunder Bay, Ontario.
Unfortunately, the cancer had spread to his lungs and now he needed medical treatment.
When his run ended, Terry had made it only halfway across the huge country.
But he had inspired many people. And his dream to raise money for cancer research came true.
He had managed to raise over 24 million dollars!
Terry also received many awards, including the Order of Canada, a high honor given to people who try to make the world a better place.
He was the youngest person ever to receive this award.
On June 28, 1981, at the age of 22, Terry Fox died.
But he still lives in the hearts of Canadian people as a great hero.
His story and amazing accomplishments have been celebrated in books and movies,
and across Canada, there are buildings, roads, ships, and even schools named after him.
Today the Terry Fox Foundation continues his race by raising money to help find a cure for cancer.
Marie Curie was a brilliant physicist and the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
She was also the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes and receive them in two different fields.
These achievements are even more incredible since few women were scientists during her lifetime.
Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska on November 7, 1867, in Warsaw, Poland.
Manya, as she was called by her parents, grew up in a family that valued education.
Her father, a math and physics teacher, taught his five children how to use scientific equipment.
Manya graduated from school early, around the age of 15.
Manya and her sister Bronya wanted to continue their studies, but women could not attend universities in Poland.
Instead they participated in the Flying University.
This was an underground organization whose members met in different locations each night to provide education and discuss politics.
Eventually Manya and Bronya decided to go to the Sorbonne, a university in Paris.
The Sorbonne was France's most prestigious university.
The sisters didn't have enough money to both attend at the same time.
So together they worked out a solution: they would take turns.
Bronya enrolled at the Sorbonne first.
While she was in Paris studying medicine, Manya stayed behind in Poland.
During this time Manya worked as a tutor and governess to help pay for Bronya's education.
Even though she wasn't going to school, Manya didn't give up on learning.
In her spare time, she continued to read about physics and chemistry.
Six years after Bronya had left, she sent good news to her sister.
Bronya had become a doctor, and she could now help pay for Manya's education at the Sorbonne.
In November 1891 Manya registered at the Sorbonne using "Marie," the French version of her name.
As a student, Marie was so busy that she hardly slept and forgot to eat!
In 1893 she earned a degree in physics, graduating first in her class.
The following year she earned another degree—this one in mathematics.
In 1894 Marie needed a laboratory to conduct scientific tests for a research project.
A friend introduced her to Pierre Curie, a young physicist with a laboratory to share.
Marie and Pierre had a lot in common, which eventually led to their marriage in July 1895.
With Pierre's encouragement, Marie decided to earn a doctoral degree.
For her research topic, she decided to continue the work of Henri Becquerel, a French physicist.
In 1896 Becquerel had found that rocks containing the element uranium give off light, or rays.
Marie wanted to find out what caused this phenomenon.
Marie discovered that Becquerel's rays were caused by changes in the atoms that make up the rocks.
Up until then scientists had believed that atoms could not change their form.
Marie called this phenomenon radioactivity.
Pierre was heavily involved in Marie's research.
Together they investigated whether other matter had radioactivity.
Their work led them to the discovery of two new elements: polonium and radium.
Marie published her research on radioactivity and the discovery of polonium and radium all in 1898.
The year 1903 was an important one for Marie.
She became the first woman to earn a doctoral degree in France.
At the end of the year, she became the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize.
She shared this Nobel Prize for Physics with Henri Becquerel and her husband, Pierre.
Sadly, in 1906, Pierre died in an accident while crossing a street.
Marie was heartbroken, but she was determined to continue on with her work.
The physics department at the Sorbonne offered Marie her husband's job as professor.
She accepted, becoming the university's first female professor.
In 1911 Marie received her second Nobel Prize, this time for chemistry, which made her a worldwide celebrity.
Despite her fame Marie kept her focus on research.
She began to explore ways to use radium to benefit others.
During World War I, she expanded the use of x-ray machines to diagnose medical conditions, and trained nurses to use them.
With the help of the French government, she also created "little Curies."
These were portable x-ray machines that could be used to examine injured soldiers immediately on the battlefield.
After World War I ended, Marie's health declined.
Scientists had not yet discovered that exposure to radioactive material was dangerous and could cause many illnesses.
Working with radioactive materials for decades had damaged Marie's health.
She died in 1934 at the age of 66.
Marie Curie's discoveries led to many of today's technologies.
Radioactivity is used to treat cancer, make electricity, and produce heat.
Her discoveries in physics and chemistry have greatly influenced science and the way we live.
For nearly four thousand years, the Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on earth.
At 147 meters tall, the pyramid has impressive height.
But it looks puny next to the tallest human-made structures today: skyscrapers.
Every day in cities around the world, millions of people go to work in towers made of steel and glass.
These modern structures demonstrate the best in construction technology and engineering skills.
Modern cities surely could not function without them.
People first began building skyscrapers in the nineteenth century.
Many cities were rapidly growing, and space in downtown areas was in high demand.
There was nowhere to build but up, so smaller buildings were demolished and replaced by taller buildings.
But the heights of these tall buildings were limited by the materials and technologies of their time.
Before skyscrapers, tall structures were rarely built for people to live or work in.
Few buildings were taller than five stories because people had to climb so many stairs.
Elevators at the time were meant for freight, not people.
They were seen to be unsafe.
If the cable that held the elevator snapped, the elevator would fall, killing those inside.
In 1852 Elisha Otis invented the safety elevator, which solved the problem of how to transport people up and down tall buildings.
Otis' new safety elevator had mechanical locks that automatically held the elevator firmly in place if the cable snapped.
While Elisha Otis was improving the elevator, other inventors were hard at work improving water pumps.
As cities expanded and their suburbs grew, more powerful pumps were needed to provide water to distant areas.
Eventually pumps were invented that could supply water across greater horizontal distances.
They were also powerful enough to pump water vertically to greater heights.
These pumps were essential for skyscrapers, which needed efficient plumbing.
Another factor that limited a building's height at the time were building materials.
Traditional materials like stone and brick were too heavy.
When stone or brick layers are piled too high, their combined weight will crush the bottom layers.
Wood was light but lacked the necessary strength.
Steel was an ideal material. With steel beams, buildings could be built around a metal frame instead of stone walls.
Finally in the 1850s, manufacturers developed a process for mass-producing steel.
This made steel available in the quantities needed for a skyscraper.
With these inventions, buildings soared higher than ever before.
But architects and engineers hadn't solved every design problem.
The design and construction of new buildings brought unforeseen challenges.
For example, strong winds could cause a tall building to sway back and forth.
Designers eventually built a strong central core of steel around the main elevator shaft of a building.
This prevented the building from shaking.
The core also made the skyscraper stable and more rigid.
Windows were another challenge because ordinary glass presented a danger.
If a window broke, large pieces of sharp glass would fall to the ground and injure people below.
The invention of tempered glass, or safety glass, solved this problem.
Safety glass was stronger than ordinary glass, and when it broke, it shattered into small pieces with rounded edges.
By the twentieth century, New York City was famous for its skyscrapers.
The city's skyline was continually being changed by the race to build the tallest skyscraper.
In 1930 the 283-meter Bank of Manhattan Building became the tallest building in the world.
It was taller than the rival Chrysler Building, which was still under construction.
However, the surprise addition of a tall spire to the Chrysler Building increased the building's height to 319 meters.
The Chrysler Building gained the title of the world's tallest building.
The Bank of Manhattan Building had only held the distinction for a month.
But the Chrysler Building's record was not undisputed.
The spire and many of the Chrysler Building's top floors were unoccupied.
But the Bank of Manhattan Building's highest occupied floors were higher than those in the Chrysler Building.
Some argued that the Bank of Manhattan Building still held the record.
By 1931 the arguments on both sides became pointless when the Empire State Building was completed.
At 443 meters tall, it was undeniably the tallest building in the world.
Its record was not broken until 1972.
New skyscrapers are still being built all over the world.
Though not world-record breakers, skyscrapers over five hundred meters tall have been built in China, Korea, and the Middle East.
In 2009 the 828-meter tall Burj Khalifa in Dubai became the tallest building in the world.
Thanks to advances in materials and technology, today's skyscrapers stand many times higher than the giant Egyptian pyramids.
And architects and engineers keep dreaming about even taller structures.
Future human-made structures will likely reshape the urban landscape—just as the first skyscrapers did over a hundred years ago.

episodes.title: Anne Frank: A Diary of Hope

subtitle.text: Anne Frank turned thirteen on June 12, 1942.
Her father, Otto, gave her a special present.
It was a diary that had a red-and-white cloth cover and a small lock.
It was exactly what Anne had wanted.
She had even pointed it out to her father in a shop window the day before.
It was the perfect birthday gift for a girl who loved to write.
In her diary Anne wrote about her life and her family.
She named the diary Kitty, writing to it as if speaking to a friend.
Anne was born in Germany in 1929.
At that time Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party were gaining power in Germany.
Hitler was a dictator who wanted to eliminate all Jewish people.
Though Anne's family was not very religious, they were Jewish, which made living in Germany dangerous.
In 1934 Otto moved his family to Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
Otto was a director at a food company.
The family lived a normal, peaceful life in Amsterdam.
In 1939 World War II began when Hitler invaded Poland.
The following year Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands, once again putting the Franks in danger.
By 1942 the situation in the Netherlands was frightening, which Anne described in her diary.
Many Jewish people were sent to concentration camps, where they were forced to work and live in horrible conditions.
Those who went to the camps were never seen again.
Jewish people were not allowed to leave the Netherlands, so Otto came up with a plan to keep his family safe.
When the time came, he would hide his family in the back rooms of his warehouse.
The time came on July 5, 1942.
Anne's sister, Margot, was summoned to a camp.
The family quickly packed up their important belongings and moved into the back rooms of the warehouse.
These rooms were known as the secret annex.
Along with the Franks, another Jewish family and a man hid in the annex.
Only six trusted helpers knew about the secret annex, including a family friend named Miep.
She had worked for Otto and became close with Anne.
The helpers sneaked food and supplies to the people in hiding.
They had to be extremely careful.
If they were caught, they would be sent to a concentration camp too.
Living in the secret annex was not easy.
Anne and her family had to be very quiet during the day.
They never went outside and couldn't use lights at night.
To pass the time, Anne wrote about daily life in the secret annex.
She complained about the awful food and wrote about the arguments among people.
She hoped to publish her diary after the war and even revised her earlier writing.
The diary gives a full picture of a wise, honest, and hopeful young girl.
In one entry she wrote: "I still believe, in spite of everything, that people are truly good at heart."
Anne's entries also tracked the progress of the war.
The annex's occupants quietly listened to the radio and heard news from the helpers.
Anne was hopeful in 1944 when she learned that British and American soldiers recaptured France from Hitler.
Anne wrote her last entry on August 1, 1944.
Three days later German officers discovered the secret annex.
Its occupants were arrested and sent to Auschwitz, a concentration camp in Poland.
Otto was immediately separated from his family.
In October, Anne and Margot were sent to another camp in Germany, Bergen-Belsen, leaving their mother behind.
She died soon after.
By early 1945 Anne and Margot had fallen ill in the camp's unhealthy conditions.
Both sisters died in February 1945.
Two months later, British and Canadian soldiers freed the camp.
Of the eight people who had hid in the secret annex, only Otto survived.
Heartbroken by the loss of his family, he traveled back to Amsterdam.
Miep had found Anne's diary and saved it.
As Otto read his daughter's words, he felt her come alive again.
He decided to fulfill his daughter's wish to publish her diary.
In 1947 the diary was first published in Dutch.
Later it was translated and published in many countries around the world.
It quickly became a symbol of hope and survival, and a testament to the horrors of evil.

episodes.title: A Magical Castle Tour through Time

subtitle.text: Tyler waited in front of a huge stone gate while his parents bought tickets for a tour of Alnwick Castle.
He had been looking forward to seeing the medieval castle where scenes from the Harry Potter movies had been filmed.
The ancient stone castle looked impressive, but Tyler felt disappointed.
"This doesn't look like Hogwarts," he thought.
Hogwarts was the name of Harry Potter's awesome-looking wizard school.
"Hello!" A woman suddenly appeared in front of him, dressed in a robe just like a student from Hogwarts.
She looked oddly familiar.
The woman grinned. "Potter fans always expect to see Hogwarts when they arrive.
But most of what you see on-screen is really a model or special effects.
Don't be too disappointed though—Alnwick has plenty of magic.
I'm Edwina, and I'll show you around."
Edwina waved a wand, and fog filled the air.
When it cleared, Tyler was surrounded by people dressed in medieval clothing, and the castle's stone walls were now made of wood!
"Where are we?" Tyler murmured.
"Alnwick Castle," Edwina said.
"We're touring the castle during the eleventh century, when castles were built of wood, not stone.
Castle-builders constructed the main building of a castle on top of a hill and enclosed the castle grounds with a large wooden wall." Tyler
wrinkled his nose. "Did wood offer much protection?" "Wooden
castles were actually strong. But
for even more protection, builders dug ditches called moats around the hill and outside the walls. The
moats were often filled with water." Tyler
looked around the lively yard where blacksmiths were hammering weapons, and servants were milling wheat. Suddenly
a loud horn blasted, and a drawbridge was yanked up. Then
soldiers with bows and arrows ran along the walls. "What's
going on?" Tyler cried. "An
attack," Edwina said. "In
the early part of the medieval period, nobles had more power than their monarchs and ruled their lands from their castles. Nobles
were often at war with each other, or their monarchs, and battles were frequent—and violent. But
don't worry—we're about to leave." She
waved her wand again, and Tyler heaved a sigh of relief. The
wooden wall had turned back to stone, and the soldiers were gone. The
castle yard was still full of activity, but now a large stone building stood on the hill. "Come
on," Edwina said, "let's go see inside. As
time went on, castles evolved," she explained. "By
the twelfth century, castle-builders were mainly using stone. Here,
in the fourteenth century, Alnwick took its present shape. Castles
became important social centers under the feudal system, which was the way that society was organized during the medieval period. Monarchs
had more power now, but they shared it with nobles in exchange for support and military service. Nobles,
in turn, let peasants live on their land in exchange for taxes and military service. Castles
also provided protection for the surrounding community in times of war." Tyler
followed Edwina inside the building. It was dark and stony, just like the castle's exterior. "Eventually
nobles lost power as monarchs developed central governments. Wars
became less frequent, and castles were no longer vital for a kingdom's defenses. England's
feudal system officially ended in 1660. Many
castles in the British Isles were abandoned or torn down, but some, like Alnwick, continued to be occupied." Edwina
flicked her wand, and the castle transformed again. Tyler
gasped at the marble walls and crystal chandeliers. "Only
the rich could afford to live in a castle," Edwina said. "But
even though castle owners installed running water, gas, and electricity, living in a castle wasn't easy. Maintaining
such old, large buildings was expensive, so many families gave up their castles in the twentieth century. Some castles
found other uses and became hospitals, prisons, or museums. Alnwick was
used by schools and colleges." Tyler followed
Edwina outdoors along a path that led toward the gate. "Today Alnwick
is still a private home," she said. "As an
intact medieval castle, it's also a tourist attraction and popular filming location." She stopped
and gestured toward a large grassy area. "This is
where we filmed a broom-flying lesson scene." " We
?" Tyler repeated, confused. Just then it hit him . . .
Edwina laughed at his startled expression. "I was an extra in one of the Harry Potter movies!"
"That's why you look familiar!"
Edwina nodded. "Production companies often hire local people as extras, and I was one of them."
With a smile, she flicked the wand again—and disappeared!
Tyler blinked. "What just happened?" he thought, shaking his head.
"Tyler! We got the tickets!" Mom called, waving him over.
Dad scratched his head. "Are you sure this is the right castle? It doesn't look like Hogwarts."
Tyler smiled. "The filmmakers used lots of special effects.
But don't worry, Dad, I've been . . . uh, looking around.
And the castle is definitely magical. Let's go see it!"

episodes.title: The Native Americans and the Buffalo

subtitle.text: Hi, my name is Donna. My Comanche name is Dawn of the Sun because I was born when the sun was rising.
I live on the edge of the Great Plains of North America, a huge, flat, grass-covered land in the middle of the continent.
My ancestors, the Comanche tribe, have been living on, or near, these plains for three hundred years.
My mother gave me a necklace made from buffalo teeth.
It was passed down to her from my grandmother, who got it from her mother.
When I put on this necklace, I imagine what the plains were like in my great-grandmother's time.
In those days buffalo roamed the plains.
Sometimes the herds were so huge, the land appeared black!
And it was amazing to experience a buffalo stampede.
The earth shook as the animals galloped by, and their pounding hooves sounded like thunder!
My people once followed the buffalo as they traveled across the plains.
We lived in tepees made of buffalo hide, which were easy to put up, take down, and carry around.
We had great respect for the buffalo.
They were considered sacred, a powerful symbol of food and shelter.
Did you know that the buffalo is the largest land animal in North America─it can weigh over 900 kilograms!
Buffalo are also called American bison and are part of the cow family.
They travel as a herd, which means they sleep, eat, and move together.
When the seasons change, they migrate to different areas.
Before a buffalo hunt, my people took time to thank the buffalo.
A medicine man offered prayers and sang songs, to make the hunt a success.
The men in our tribe performed a sun dance, wearing buffalo masks and moving like the buffalo.
As they danced they carried their favorite spears, to bring them luck on the hunt.
We told stories about great hunts or brave hunters.
After the hunt the camp bustled with activity.
Everyone was busy with something to do.
The medicine man offered the best part of the meat to the Great Spirit as a token of thanks, and then buried it in the ground.
The women prepared the remaining meat, leaving some strips to hang and dry for use in the cold winter months.
The meat was shared among all the members of the tribe.
But the hides were most prized, and were claimed by the hunter's family.
It took a lot of work to prepare the hides.
The women had to scrape off the flesh and dry the hides in the sun.
With the fur left on, the thick winter hides were used to make warm caps, mittens, robes, and blankets.
The summer hides were used for leather, so the hair was scraped off, and they were smoked over fires to make them waterproof.
Then they could be made into tepees, clothing, and moccasins.
Many accessories and utensils could also be made from the buffalo.
We enjoyed wearing necklaces, like my great-grandmother's, made from buffalo teeth.
Some of the buffalo organs were used as containers— the stomach became a water jug.
Horns were carved to make cups and spoons.
And the bones were shaped into many useful tools, such as knives, paintbrushes, and spears.
Even though life was hard for us, we still had fun.
Comanche children made rattles from buffalo hooves, tying them together with cords cut from rawhide.
We made spinning tops from horns. We stuffed leftover hair into leather to make balls and dolls.
And in the winter, we loved to race down snowy hills, using buffalo ribs as sleds.
We also played with the buffalo calves, which sometimes followed us back to our camp.
We chased each other around for hours, and then fell down from exhaustion.
My people had been living this way, in harmony with the buffalo, for hundreds of years.
But then settlers from Europe came and took over our land.
They killed over fifty million buffalo, and the species almost became extinct!
By the nineteenth century there were only a few hundred of these amazing animals left.
By the 1900s people began trying to save the buffalo by increasing their numbers.
Conservationists took care of the remaining buffalo and were able to breed them.
Over time their numbers grew, and today, there are about 200,000 buffalo living on farms and ranches, and in special buffalo preserves.
I have a dream that one day I will become a teacher and educate people about the buffalo and our culture.
When the buffalo herds disappeared, we Comanches lost our main source of food, clothing, and shelter.
But each time I wear my great-grandmother's necklace, it reminds me of this sacred animal and all it brought my people.
Roads are everywhere. We use them every day but hardly think about them.
They are so much a part of daily life that the English language is full of phrases about roads.
When we say that a project "hits a bump in the road," we mean a problem has occurred,
and a person who takes "the road less traveled" has chosen an unusual way of life.
Roads developed along with human civilization, so we have to go a long way back to find a time before roads.
During the Ice Age seventy thousand years ago, humans lived in caves and hunted wild animals with weapons made of sticks and stones.
The ground was covered with snow, and hunters easily lost their way in the thick forests.
They would mark their tracks with branches so that they could find their way home.
That is how the first paths were created.
Around 10,000 BC, the earth's climate began to warm up.
Tribes of people started to live in villages, where they grew crops and kept tame animals.
They also learned how to make tools out of bronze and iron.
They needed roads to travel to each other's villages,
so they cleared paths through forests and across plains and built simple dirt roads with their tools.
They used primitive carts to carry heavy loads on these first roads.
Dirt roads, however, twisted and turned and did not last long.
Also they were not convenient in bad weather.
Rain would turn the dirt to mud, making it impossible for people or animals to pull their carts.
Roads could remain unusable for days after a heavy rain.
Over time the footsteps and wheels from all the traffic would create deep grooves in the roads.
These narrow ruts made walking and pulling carts even more difficult.
But despite all these problems, it was a long time before anyone improved on dirt roads.
The first modern roads were built at the height of the Roman Empire in the first century AD.
The Roman Empire was very powerful. It ruled over three continents and had a very large army.
In order to move their soldiers around the vast empire, the Roman emperors needed well-built roads.
Fortunately the Romans were great engineers.
The roads they built ran perfectly straight for hundreds of kilometers.
The Romans built their roads from stones instead of dirt, and laid gravel and cement over the stones to give the roads a hard, smooth surface.
They even carefully shaped their roads so that the center was a little higher than the edges.
That way, rainwater would not collect in pools but would run off to the sides.
Roman roads were the first to have a drainage system to keep them from flooding.
Another famous saying is that "all roads lead to Rome," and during the time of the Roman Empire, this was certainly true.
But it remained true for long after and, in some ways, it is still true today.
The Roman roads were so convenient that everyone used them, not just the soldiers.
People traveled from town to town, traded goods, and sent messages using the Roman roads.
Villages and towns located along the roads grew larger, while towns farther away became smaller.
The Romans built their roads so well that many of them lasted until the nineteenth century!
More than a thousand years after the last Roman emperor died, people were still using the straight, durable roads that once connected the Roman Empire.
In fact, many of Europe's modern highways follow those same routes today.
By the time of the Industrial Revolution in the late eighteenth century, new road technologies were needed.
Goods manufactured in factories had to be transported to and from great, crowded cities like London and Paris.
The train was invented, and people began to travel much more than before.
An engineer from Scotland named John McAdam revolutionized the way roads were built.
His method, called the macadam, is still used today.
He crushed stone into three specific sizes and built his roads in layers,
using the largest stones for the bottom layer and the smallest stones for the top layer.
By wetting the road and then compacting it with a heavy roller, the stones locked together to create a firm surface.
Macadam roads were more durable, less expensive, and easier to build, but they were very dusty.
With the invention of the automobile, a smoother, cleaner surface was needed.
Today paved roads are covered in asphalt.
Asphalt was first used in France in 1824 on the Champs-Elysees boulevard in Paris.
Asphalt was not popular at first because it was rough, but a few years later, a man called Edward de Smedt perfected it.
In 1872 he produced a higher-grade asphalt, and the first street to be paved using his asphalt was Fifth Avenue in New York.
By the turn of the twentieth century, cars, bicycles, and motorbikes were everywhere.
After World War II cities were getting overcrowded, and people began to experience the first traffic jams.
The first highways were built in the 1960s.
Highways are designed for safe, fast travel.
They have no traffic lights, no stop signs, and no parking.
Today highways are the most popular method of ground travel.
Even though advances in road-building have greatly improved travel, many cities are now polluted and overcrowded with traffic.
And traffic jams are not just bad for drivers, they are also bad for the environment.
Cars and trucks contribute to unhealthy smog and global warming.
While new electric and hybrid cars are much less polluting, many cities have decided to make parts of their downtown off limits to cars.
The historic downtown of Copenhagen in Denmark is Europe's oldest and largest car-free zone.
People walk its streets just like people did on the first roads thousands of years ago.
Roads have been part of human civilization since hunters first marked their footsteps in the snow.
So whether we travel by foot, by car, or in some new vehicle of the future, wherever we go, there will always be roads.

episodes.title: Thomas Edison: The Wizard of Menlo Park

subtitle.text: Do you ever wonder who invented the light bulb, the movie camera, and the record player?
Can you imagine your life without any of these items today?
The person we have to thank for all of them is Thomas Edison.
He created hundreds of inventions in his lifetime that we continue to use today.
Thomas Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, in 1847.
He was the youngest in a household of seven children.
When he was young, Thomas was a very curious boy.
He always asked questions about everything around him.
He wanted to know where things came from.
His curiosity often got him in trouble.
One day he asked his mother why the hen sat on her eggs, and she told him it was because the hen was hatching her eggs.
Without thinking, Thomas sat on a pile of eggs to try to hatch them too and broke them all.
Another time he was curious about how fire worked, so he set his father's barn on fire to see what would happen.
The barn burned down. His father was very angry with him and punished him by giving him a thrashing in the town square.
When young Thomas started school, he was so curious that he disturbed his classmates by constantly interrupting the teacher with questions.
For this reason Thomas was sent home to be taught by his mother.
Thomas' mother understood her son's curiosity and patiently let his imagination grow.
Thomas loved to conduct experiments. He set up a laboratory in his parents' attic and filled it with different chemicals.
Strange smells, sounds, and even small explosions would often come out of the attic.
Thomas wasn't homeschooled for very long. When he turned 16, he got a job as a train boy on the local train.
He sold candy, newspapers, fruit, and sandwiches to the passengers.
He loved his job because he got to set up a small laboratory in the baggage compartment, where he was able to experiment during the long train rides.
The conductor was not very happy about this, and after Thomas lit a small fire in the compartment, he was let go from his job.
This did not faze the young inventor; he soon found a new passion—the telegraph machine.
In the 1860s there was a great need for telegraph operators throughout the United States.
Thomas learned the telegraph code and was quickly hired, and worked as a telegraph operator for six years.
But he was not content with the telegraph machine of the day.
He wanted to improve it so that one machine could be used to both send and receive messages.
He worked hard on his invention at night, often falling asleep at his desk.
Finally he was able to improve the telegraph and sold the patent for his new machine to the Western Union company.
Encouraged by the sale, and now with money to support his work, Thomas began experimenting on new inventions.
He set up a small laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey.
He was busy working on a new machine that would record sound.
The telephone had recently been invented by Alexander Graham Bell, and Thomas was interested in this device.
He wanted to find ways to record the sounds that came out of the telephone.
His new invention was called a phonograph and would become the prototype for the modern record player. It was an instant success.
But Thomas did not stop there. His new passion became finding ways to use electricity.
In those days people used oil lamps to light their homes.
They were smoky and dangerous, and the light was not very strong.
Thomas was convinced that by using electricity he could produce brighter, more uniform light that would be easier to use.
He experimented long into the night. He often took short naps with his head on his desk so that he could continue to work.
Thomas filled hundreds of books with notes, and at one time,
said that he had considered over three thousand theories for creating light from electricity.
Finally he had a breakthrough. He found that he could pass electricity through a cotton thread placed inside a glass bulb.
While other inventors had worked on light-bulb designs,
Edison was the first to create one that lasted for a long time and was cheap enough to be easily mass-produced.
He installed his version of the electric light in his house in Menlo Park.
People from all over flocked to see Edison's new invention, and Thomas became an overnight celebrity.
People began calling him the Wizard of Menlo Park.
Soon towns all over the world lit up their houses and streets with electric lights.
Even though Thomas now had enough money to retire, he continued to work on new inventions.
He invented a Kinetoscope, a light box that showed moving pictures, which later became the movie camera.
He also worked on developing an electric car, electric batteries, a cement mixer, and a copying machine.
In his lifetime Thomas Edison held 1,093 patents and would have continued to invent if he had not fallen sick.
He died on October 18, 1931, at the age of 84.
In his honor the lights all over the United States were turned off on the night of his funeral.
Thomas Edison left a great legacy. Our everyday life would not be the same if it were not for his curious mind.
His inventions are still used today by many people on the planet.

episodes.title: Castles of the Middle Ages: Places of Legend

subtitle.text: Miles and his little brother Adrian stood on the deck of a tour boat.
"Look! Do you see that castle?" called out Adrian.
"Of course! We are in the land of castles!" said Miles.
The two boys were taking a tour with their parents down the Rhine River in Germany.
The Rhine River is famous for all the ancient castles along its shores.
Until that day, the only castle the boys had ever seen was at Disneyland.
But the Disneyland castle was only a copy of a real castle.
The boys were looking forward to seeing a castle up close—a real one, where people used to live, fight battles, and have adventures.
Thousands of castles were built during the Middle Ages.
In those days most people lived all their lives in the same place where they were born.
They lived a simple life and worked in the fields; they were called peasants.
The people who owned the land were called lords, and they lived in castles.
Many of the lords were at war with each other over land and money, and were often fighting.
In order to protect themselves and their families, they built castles with thick stone walls, high on hills and mountaintops.
Some castles were big and luxurious; others were smaller and simpler.
Many different people lived in the castle with the lord and his family.
Each of these people had a specific job.
There were cooks, servants, dressmakers, blacksmiths, and musicians.
Most lords also had a personal army of soldiers living with them who were always ready to fight.
They were called knights. Knights fought with swords and long spears.
They wore heavy suits of metal armor and rode large, powerful horses into battle.
As the tour boat got closer to the castle, the guide on the boat explained that this was the Marksburg Castle, near the town of Braubach.
It was built in the twelfth century and has never been destroyed.
"Let's go see," said Miles.
The boat docked near the path that led to the castle.
After the boys walked up the hill, they faced a huge gate in a high stone wall.
Most castles were built the same way; the gate in the outer wall was always strongly defended.
Many castles were also surrounded by a ditch full of water called a moat.
A small drawbridge that led to the gate was the only way across the water.
Whenever an enemy approached, the drawbridge could be raised from safe inside the castle walls.
The boys noticed that the castle walls were several feet thick.
The thick walls protected the castle from cannon attacks.
Also, soldiers could stand on top of these walls and attack the enemy below with arrows, stones, and other weapons.
Almost all castles had tall watchtowers from where knights would look out for approaching invaders.
Some castles also had prisons, called dungeons, deep beneath the ground for captured enemy soldiers.
Inside, the castle was very dark and cold.
Castles had few fireplaces, and the rooms were too big to heat easily.
The boys entered a large room with a long wooden table.
The room was lit by candles in chandeliers hanging from the ceiling.
This was the main hall, where the lord and his family had dinner.
At night they liked to host rich feasts while musicians and storytellers entertained them.
Miles could picture it all in his mind; it was just like something out of a storybook.
The legends and histories of castles have always made good stories.
In fact, the legends of many castles have been passed down from generation to generation.
One of the most famous is the legend of Fyvie Castle in Scotland.
For centuries people knew that a secret room with a great treasure was hidden somewhere in the castle.
But there was a curse on the room: whoever found it would die, and his wife would become blind.
According to the story, a man named General Adrian finally found the hidden room but died shortly after from unknown causes.
His wife soon became blind. Another man called Sir Maurice Duff tried to find the room, but while exploring the castle, he fell and broke his leg.
Strangely, his wife developed an eye illness for the rest of her life.
Another famous legend is connected to the Frankenstein Castle in Germany.
A terrible dragon terrorized the peasants and lords in the area for years.
The only way to keep the dragon away was to sacrifice a beautiful girl from the nearby village.
When a girl named Anne Marie was given to the dragon, a knight from the castle, who was secretly in love with her, came to the rescue.
After a fierce battle, the knight set Anne Marie free.
But just as he killed the dragon with his sword, the dragon twisted its poison tail around and wounded the brave knight in the leg.
He died soon after, but the legend of the knight still lives on in the Frankenstein Castle.
"Boys? Where are you?" Adrian and Miles heard someone call.
"The boat is about to leave." They turned and saw their mother looking for them.
"Hurry, let's go!" Miles said and grabbed his brother's hand.
They left the main hall and ran back down the hill.
"When I grow up I want to be a knight," said Adrian when they reached the boat.
Sadly, there are no more knights or lords, but the castles they left behind tell a great story—of a time long ago full of adventure.

episodes.title: The Vikings: Deadly Invaders, Bold Explorers

subtitle.text: In 793 a monk described a frightening attack on a monastery in England.
Suddenly giant men jumped from the long ships.
They were a head taller than any of us, and some had bright red hair.
They had all manner of armor and weapons, and they killed every monk they saw, even though we had no weapons. Luckily I escaped.
When I returned to the monastery, anything made of silver or gold was gone—everything of value. Who were these strange, terrifying warriors? The
warriors were Vikings. From
the eighth to the eleventh century, the Vikings raided the coasts of Europe during an era now called the Viking Age. England,
France, Scotland, and Ireland were prey to their attacks. The
Vikings came from the Scandinavian countries in northern Europe now known as Norway, Sweden, and Denmark. They
were also called Norsemen, which means men from the north. Viking
warriors stole whatever they found and killed many people, usually attacking with iron swords and large battle-axes. They
wore skillfully made metal armor, and for defense, they carried round wooden shields with a center made of iron. Today
many pictures show Vikings wearing helmets with horns, but this idea is an error that began in the nineteenth century. Most
Viking warriors actually wore simple iron caps. At
home the Vikings were farmers. They
kept cattle, pigs, ducks, and chickens, and their farmlands produced crops like wheat and rye, as well as vegetables. Early
spring was a busy time as they prepared their crops for planting. With
help from slaves and servants, they plowed and fertilized the fields and planted seeds for grains. And
then, after this spring work was finished, the Vikings left to attack foreign lands. The
Vikings set sail in their boats to raid monasteries and villages for precious metals and for people to enslave. Carved
from wood, their "longships" enabled the Vikings to travel swiftly and efficiently. The
ships were light and long, with high curves at the front and back. They
had oars along their entire length and a square sail above, so
the Vikings could travel on the sea and then use the oars to make a speedy attack. Many
of the ships also had a tall, fierce-looking dragon carved into their prows. When
villagers saw one of these ships approaching, they often fled in terror! Because
their boats were shallow, the Vikings were also able to travel inland by river. Their
trade routes reached deep into Europe.
France, Poland, and Russia were all part of the dynamic world of Viking commerce.
Eventually the Vikings realized that many of the countries they raided (or traded with) were better for farming than their own homeland.
They began to establish forts or settlements, and from these strongholds, they continued their raids and conquered new territory.
The Vikings' ships were small, but they were very sturdy, which allowed the Vikings to travel to faraway places and become great explorers.
Iceland was first settled by Vikings.
When the famous Viking Erik the Red was banished from Iceland, he set sail in his longship in search of adventure.
He discovered Greenland, and one of his sons, Leif Erikson, was the first European to reach North America.
Leif sailed west of Greenland and discovered Baffin Island, Labrador, and Newfoundland almost five hundred years before Columbus reached America.
Strangely enough, despite their warlike manner, the Vikings often adapted to, and joined the people they conquered.
Over time the Vikings who conquered England became English;
the Vikings who conquered Normandy quickly became part of its native French-speaking population.
While the Vikings were raiders and pirates, they were also traders and merchants.
Their trading ships carried fur, ivory, amber, and slaves.
The Vikings were superb metalworkers, so they exported swords and other weapons.
And some Vikings worked as mercenaries. They were never a unified group; instead they were separate bands of sea pirates.
The Vikings are often portrayed as barbaric savages, but they were well organized and had a written language called Runic.
The Vikings’ mastery of this written language helped them conquer many opponents because it allowed them to send messages with ease.
Much of their heritage survives today in the Norse sagas, which describe the adventures of their heroes and gods.
These great legends inspired famous operas and poems, written many centuries after the Viking Age ended.
The Viking heritage is still remembered today.
In Scandinavia there are several Viking ship museums,
where people can see restored Viking ships and admire the amazing craftsmanship of these bold sailors.
And many cities hold annual Viking festivals.
People can live and dress as Vikings, and craft weapons and jewelry using traditional Viking methods.
Some people even participate in mock Viking battles!
During the Viking age, the "men from the north" explored distant lands—and terrorized many people.
With their longships and thirst for adventure, they left a permanent mark on both ship technology and European history.
Many music lovers and scholars consider Ludwig van Beethoven one of the greatest composers who ever lived.
It's especially amazing that Beethoven composed many of his musical masterpieces after losing his hearing!
Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn, Germany, in 1770.
Both his father and grandfather were court musicians—musicians hired to play for royalty. Beethoven’s
father was determined to teach his young son to play music, and to turn him into a prodigy. According
to many stories, Beethoven was often crying as he practiced, and his father made him work very hard, often until late at night. When
Beethoven was almost 12, he published his first composition. He
had also been appointed as an assistant organist at the court—an impressive job for such a young musician. It was
around this time that Beethoven left school and devoted himself entirely to music. As a
result, he was never a very good speller. His letters
show that he often made simple grammatical errors, even later in his life. As Beethoven
began earning money from his music, his family grew more dependent upon his income. The Beethovens
had once been wealthy, but the father was an alcoholic. His serious
drinking problem had led the family into financial decline. When
Beethoven turned 18 years old, the court decided to send him to Vienna, which was the center of the music world at that time. Beethoven
wanted to stay in Vienna and study with the great composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. But
back in Bonn, disaster struck. His mother fell ill and died, and Beethoven had to return home to Bonn. The
next years were probably a very stressful time in the Beethoven household. Beethoven’s
father was still drinking, and Beethoven had two younger brothers who needed his financial support. Beethoven’s
life was very busy as he tried to take care of his family and practice and develop his music. Yet
it was also a good time for his career as he took on more responsibilities at court. He
also expanded his social circle with other musicians and some prosperous friends. In
1790 an important European political figure—the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, Joseph II—died, and
Beethoven was invited to compose the funeral ode. This
was a huge honor for a young composer. While
Beethoven's composition was never played at the emperor's funeral, it
did eventually attract the attention of another well-known composer—Joseph Haydn. By
1792 Beethoven was traveling back to Vienna to study with Haydn as well as other composers. During
this time Beethoven continued to compose music. His
compositions were very different from anything anyone had heard before. Beethoven
included new sounds and paired up instruments in new and creative ways. He
also became known in Vienna for his playing of the piano; he received many invitations to play at the homes of noble families and aristocrats. By
the time Beethoven was around 28 years old, disaster had struck again—he realized he was losing his hearing. Over
the years he became completely deaf, sometimes isolating himself from others, and growing bitter about his condition. Even
though he could no longer hear his compositions being played, Beethoven kept writing music. He
often wandered country roads in villages near Vienna, and in sketchbooks, he wrote down his ideas. His
music grew more sensitive and powerful because of his personal struggles. Beethoven
never had luck finding love, and this added to his loneliness and dark spirit. His
piece Moonlight Sonata is regarded as one of his most beautiful works. It
is believed that it was inspired by the tragic love he felt for a girl he couldn’t marry. Beethoven's
nine symphonies are also considered masterpieces. A
symphony is a long musical work played by an orchestra.
Beethoven wrote complicated compositions that evoke many different moods and feelings.
Each symphony has a different theme and expresses a different emotion.
His Symphony No. 3 was written in honor of Napoleon, whom Beethoven admired for a time.
Symphony No. 6 was inspired by the beauty found in nature.
In one section Beethoven has woodwind instruments imitate the sounds of nightingales, cuckoos, and quails.
His most popular symphony is probably his final one—Symphony No. 9.
It is a very powerful piece of music, one in which Beethoven uses both an orchestra and a chorus of singers.
When it was first played, the audience loved it so much, they clapped for a very long time after the concert ended.
Because he was deaf, Beethoven was completely unaware of the thunderous applause.
Finally someone turned him in the direction of the audience so he could see their enthusiastic clapping and cheering.
Ludwig van Beethoven died in Vienna on March 26, 1827 at age 57.
He left an incredible musical legacy that includes some of the most important musical works of all time.
It is hard to believe that he created many of these great works without being able to hear a single note.
It was the beauty of the world that inspired Pierre-Auguste Renoir.
He loved to paint families strolling in the park, young couples dancing at a ball, and children playing in the sun.
He began as a humble painter decorating porcelain vases,
and eventually he became one of the world's most significant painters and the father of Impressionism.
Renoir was born in 1841 in Limoges, a small French town.
His father was a tailor and his mother a dressmaker.
When Renoir was four years old, his family moved to Paris in search of a better life.
The family lived very close to the Louvre, a large museum with the richest collection of art in France.
The young Renoir spent long days there, looking at the old masters' paintings, deeply inspired by their beauty.
His favorite artist was Peter Paul Rubens, whose art continued to influence him throughout his life.
As a young schoolboy, Renoir covered his schoolbooks with drawings.
His parents urged him to put his artistic talents to use and helped him get a job at a porcelain factory.
There Renoir learned to paint delicate flower patterns on porcelain vases.
He was a fast learner and soon became a very successful painter.
His career came to an end, however, when a new mechanical process for printing designs onto chinaware was introduced.
To earn a living, he copied onto women's fans the paintings he had seen at the Louvre as a child.
Then he sold the fans on the street.
But he knew that he wanted to do more with his life he dreamed of becoming an artist and creating paintings just like the ones he was copying.
In 1861 Renoir was penniless but determined to become an artist.
He enrolled in an art class in the studio of Charles Gleyre, where he met other struggling artists who would become his lifelong friends.
Together with Claude Monet, Alfred Sisley, and Camille Pissaro he would paint all day,
and then in the evenings, they would gather at cafes to discuss art.
One of their favorite gathering places was the Inn of Mother Anthony, which Renoir immortalized in one of his paintings.
The young artists were searching for new ways of painting and soon became known as the Impressionists.
The Impressionists believed in a new way of seeing.
They used many brushstrokes of different colors right next to each other on the canvas.
By this method, they captured a feeling of movement and light in their paintings.
Instead of smoothing the surface of the painting like artists before them, the Impressionists would leave traces of their brushstrokes visible.
They also went outside to paint, instead of staying in their studios.
The Impressionists packed their paintbrushes, paints, and easels and set out into nature, searching for inspiring landscapes.
This period of his studies was a difficult one for Renoir.
With almost no money, he often thought about giving up, but his passion for painting kept him going.
He kept thinking of the artists from the Louvre who he admired as a young child.
His artist friends always gave him a helping hand.
His friend Bazille offered to share his studio, and his friend Monet often gave him encouraging advice.
By 1863 Renoir was still trying to find his own painting style.
He was using dark and gloomy tones that never seemed right to him.
One day he was out painting in a park when an old man came to see his work.
He said to Renoir, "Your painting is good but why do you use such dark colors?
Don't you see the beauty around you?"
Renoir realized that he could paint the world as he wished to see it.
He began using fresh and light colors.
The old man turned out to be an established painter from Paris named Narcisse Diaz.
He helped Renoir by buying him painting supplies and introducing him to art dealers.
Renoir was able to get a few commissions to paint portraits, and this eased his financial worries.
One of Renoir's favorite subjects was the life of Parisians.
He loved to paint them dancing, walking in the park, enjoying a meal, or sitting at the opera.
He wanted to express the joy he saw in everyday life.
Renoir also loved to paint people socializing.
His studio was very close to a popular dance hall in Paris, where he spent almost one year sketching and painting scenes of dancing couples.
He was fascinated with the graceful movements of women when they danced.
By the time Renoir reached his forties, he was a well-established painter in Paris.
He lived well off his portrait commissions, often painting aristocrats, art dealers, and rich patrons.
In 1883 he had his first solo exhibition in Paris.
Even though he was becoming successful, he never stopped developing his own artistic style.
He traveled to Algeria in search of new and interesting subjects and painted the exotic landscapes he found there.
At the end of his career, Renoir returned to working in a classical style, similar to the paintings he copied from the Louvre in his youth.
Even though Renoir was crippled by arthritis and almost blind, he kept painting until his death in 1919.
Through his art he created his own world full of light, happiness, and promise.
His paintings continue to bring joy and optimism to millions of people today.
"The only time I feel alive is when I'm painting."
These words were written by one of the greatest painters, Vincent van Gogh.
While van Gogh’s life was full of disappointments and tragedy, he was able to overcome these in his art.
He produced some of the most important masterpieces of all time.
In his art, van Gogh created his own world of light, hope, and happiness.
Vincent van Gogh was born in Holland in 1853.
He had a happy childhood and grew up in a small village called Groot-Zundert.
Young Vincent enjoyed playing alone in the nearby fields and often made sketches of the plants he found.
He liked to draw at an early age, but he didn’t become an artist until later in life.
Van Gogh was first an art dealer and later a church minister like his father.
He worked as an art dealer, but he was not very good at serving the public.
He was often rude to customers, and he disliked the idea of art being bought and sold.
After studying to be a minister, in 1879 van Gogh moved to Borinage, Belgium, a village of coal miners.
It was in Borinage that van Gogh started to paint.
The Potato Eaters is dark and gloomy.
Its colors communicate the hard life that the miners and their families suffered.
Vincent painted life as he saw it. He felt great kindness for the miners.
However, even though he often gave away his clothes and furniture, he was not a good minister.
Van Gogh left for Paris, the center of art and culture in Europe.
Once Vincent moved to Paris, his palette and his feelings about life changed. He had renewed energy and enthusiasm.
Instead of the old clothes he wore in Borinage, he wore a colorful scarf, a fashionable hat, and a suit.
He lived with his devoted brother Theo who was an art dealer there. He helped Vincent meet other artists.
In Paris Vincent met a group of artists called the Impressionists.
The Impressionists didn’t paint things realistically,
but instead they tried to portray emotions through the use of short brushstrokes and brilliant colors.
Vincent was inspired. He painted Bridges in Asnieres with bright colors, in the style of the Impressionists.
After two years in Paris, van Gogh longed for the countryside.
He moved from Paris to a small village called Arles in southern France.
He made a bright yellow house his home.
Van Gogh spent his days painting the nearby wheat fields in the summer sun, the local people, and his beloved yellow house.
Yellow had become van Gogh’s favorite color.
It represented all the hope, light, and happiness that he was searching for in life.
He painted fast, as if trying to capture a brief moment or feeling with his paintbrush.
He painted flowers, plum orchards, and cherry blossoms before they faded.
At Arles, he reached his artistic peak.
Around this time van Gogh became fascinated with painting sunflowers.
For him, they represented the energy and warmth of the sun.
He painted many versions of them, in different places and in different shades of yellow.
Today Sunflowers is one of the most famous paintings in the world, and it sold for $39.9 million.
It hangs behind bulletproof glass at a Japanese insurance company.
Vincent was lonely in Arles. His only friend was the local postman, Roulin.
Vincent painted eight portraits of the postman, as well as portraits of his wife and kids.
Despite his poverty, Roulin refused to be paid for letting Vincent paint him, and he often invited Vincent for dinner with his family.
Spending time with the Roulins made Vincent feel part of a family, something he had thought he would never feel again.
Van Gogh had only one friend in his village, and there were no other artists.
So he soon invited his friend, and fellow artist from Paris, Paul Gauguin, to come and work with him in Arles.
At first the two friends enjoyed each other’s company.
They made grand plans for the future and complimented and supported each other’s work,
but as time passed by, they started quarreling over their ideas about art.
It was after one big fight with Gauguin that Vincent cut off part of his ear.
He had to be taken to the hospital. Gauguin left Arles.
Van Gogh painted Self Portrait with a Bandaged Ear soon after, and it shows how miserable and sick he was.
From this time until his death, he would suffer many mental breakdowns.
Wheat Fields with Crows is one of Vincent’s last paintings.
It shows how gloomy his thoughts were.
The sky is dark, the crows appear to be flying madly toward the viewer, and the road seems to lead nowhere.
Vincent, who was usually optimistic and tried to celebrate life in his paintings, had lost hope. His illness had overtaken him.
Theo came to see him from Paris, but it was too late.
He died in his brother’s arms on July 29, 1890, at the age of 37.
He didn’t become an artist until later in life and didn’t live long,
but in the short time he painted, Vincent van Gogh created some of the most astonishing and important works of art of all time.
It's hard to imagine that the great leaders of history were once boys, but they were.
And it's hard to imagine that some boys will grow up to change history, but they can.
Imagine a very poor boy who lives with his family in one room.
Imagine that he is so thin and tall that his clothes barely fit.
Imagine that his brother dies as a baby, and his mother dies when he is nine.
Imagine this boy going to school only a few times in his life.
Now imagine him becoming the president of the United States.
As impossible as it sounds, that is exactly what happened to Abraham Lincoln.
Abraham Lincoln was a poor farm boy from Kentucky, born in 1809.
The Lincolns had very little money, and no one imagined that he would be a great leader one day.
Abraham's father, Thomas, was a carpenter and he wanted his son to become a carpenter too.
Abraham obeyed his father and learned how to carve wood, but he hoped for something different.
Abraham's mother taught her children to be cheerful and smart and to work hard.
Abraham loved books, and every day his mother read to him from the Bible.
She taught him that peace is important, unless there is something worth fighting for.
Later, as an adult, Abraham said that his mother taught him how to be a great man.
One day while Abraham was out with a horse, the horse kicked him in the head.
His body lay so still that, at first, people thought he was dead, but he recovered.
Later that same year, his mother died from milk poisoning.
It was such a surprise to the family that they didn't have a funeral until two months later.
Abraham was only nine years old, but he helped his father carve the coffin for his mother.
He remembered that her last words to him and his sister were:
"Be good and kind to your father, to each other, and to the world."
Over the next ten years, there were many more changes in Abraham's family.
His father married a new wife who had three children, and Abraham learned to love them.
Together they moved to a new state called Illinois where Abraham grew into a young man.
When Abraham became an adult, he left home to find his future.
He moved to the town of New Salem where he earned the courageous nickname of Honest Abe by defeating a group of bullies.
The Clary's Grove Boys liked to drink and start fights.
When their leader heard someone say that Abraham was smarter and stronger than any man in town, he challenged Abe to a fight.
Abraham accepted. He was tired of the bullies scaring people in the town.
Both men were good wrestlers and had quick reflexes.
For a while they twisted and clutched at each other.
Then Abe reached over his opponent, grabbed him by the neck, lifted him off the ground, and shook him like a blanket.
Since Abraham was a foot taller than most people, this wasn't hard for him.
The Clary's Grove Boys rushed towards Abe to beat him.
Abe dropped their leader and said, "If you want a fight, boys, I'll give it to you, but you must fight me one at a time."
They were surprised by Abe's courage and honesty and shook hands with him.
There would be many more battles in Abraham Lincoln's life, and each of them was for something he believed was worth fighting for.
As a lawyer, he fought for the life of a friend and proved that he was not guilty.
He fought to represent his state, arguing against the Mexican War, and he won.
He fought to serve as a senator and stood for election nine times, but never received enough votes.
In 1860 he ran for president and was elected.
At the time of his election, the southern and northern states were disagreeing about slavery,
and this discord was leading toward the Civil War.
As the president, Lincoln spoke out against slavery and the war, but when the war began, he fought to restore peace and freedom to his nation.
He made his most famous speech, the Gettysburg Address, to dedicate a grave for soldiers who had died on both sides of the war.
In all of his battles, Lincoln showed respect for the freedom of all people.
In April 1865, while attending a play in Washington, Abraham Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth,
who still disagreed with Lincoln over the war.
The great president died at the age of 56.
His life can be summed up by a verse from the Bible, his favorite book, which says,
"I have fought the good fight; I have kept the faith; I have finished the race."
One of the largest and most famous cities in the United States is San Francisco, but it hasn't always been popular.
In fact, in 1848 there were only five hundred people living there.
Only two years later in 1850—thanks to something called the Gold Rush—the city had grown to 25,000 people.
On a cold morning in January 1848, James Marshall and John Sutter were on the banks of the American River building a sawmill.
Marshall saw something glittering in the water, and when he pulled it out, he realized it was gold!
Marshall and Sutter didn't want people to stop the construction of their sawmill, so they agreed to keep the gold a secret.
Unfortunately for them Sam Brannan found out about the gold, and that is how the Gold Rush began.
Sam Brannan was a brilliant businessman. Unlike Marshall and Sutter, he knew that he could make money from gold without even digging for it.
First, Brannan bought every shovel, pan, and digging tool in San Francisco.
Then, he ran through the streets yelling, "There's gold in the American River! Gold for everyone! We'll be rich!"
Of course everyone wants to be rich.
But to get rich with gold, people need tools to mine the gold.
